battery_overview: This page analyzes a single question-and-answer exchange from the deposition. Think of it as an X-ray of the conversation — not just what was said, but what actually happened beneath the surface. Did the witness accept the attorney's framing or push back against it? Did the question open new lines of inquiry or shut them down? Did something new emerge from the exchange that neither speaker brought in alone? Each section below examines a different dimension of that exchange, building toward the two-word Pattern Declaration at the top, which is the instrument's single summary judgment of what kind of moment this was.

pattern_field.label: Pattern Declaration
pattern_field.definition: The two-word summary of this entire exchange. After analyzing five separate dimensions of the question and answer, the instrument produces a single label that names the kind of moment this was — not what was talked about, but what structurally happened. Think of it as a diagnosis rather than a description.
pattern_field.why_it_matters: When you read these two-word labels across dozens or hundreds of exchanges, patterns emerge. You start to see whether the deposition was mostly cooperative, mostly evasive, whether the witness was being led or resisting, whether the attorney was in control. A single label means little on its own — the value is in the sequence.
pattern_field.value_description: The two-word label shown is the instrument's single summary judgment of what structurally happened in this exchange — the kind of moment it was, not the topic it covered.

fields.label: Transformation
fields.definition: What actually changed between the question and the answer — not the words that were exchanged, but the shift in what is now known, established, or understood. Every question-answer pair moves something. This field names what moved.
fields.why_it_matters: Depositions are not just conversations — they are knowledge-building events. Every exchange either advances, retreats, or redirects what is known on the record. Understanding what transformed in each exchange tells you whether the deposition is moving toward or away from the facts that matter to the case.
fields.value_description: The short label shown names the shift that occurred — what moved between the question and the answer at the level of knowledge or understanding.

fields.label: Object Of Transformation
fields.definition: The specific thing that was transformed — the subject matter that got moved, clarified, reframed, or established. If Transformation tells you what happened, Object Of Transformation tells you what it happened to.
fields.why_it_matters: Knowing what was transformed is only useful if you also know what it was transformed about. This field names the target — the specific concept, fact, or question at the center of the exchange.
fields.value_description: The short label shown names the specific thing that was transformed — the subject matter that got moved, clarified, or established by this exchange.

fields.label: Scaffolding
fields.definition: The underlying structure that made this exchange possible — what held the question up, what held the answer up, and what the two together created that neither had alone. Think of it like the frame of a building: you don't see it when everything is working, but it's what keeps the exchange from collapsing.
fields.why_it_matters: When scaffolding is solid, the exchange produces reliable information. When it is weak — when the question rests on an assumption that isn't established, or the answer doesn't connect to anything real — the exchange may look productive while actually building nothing. Spotting weak scaffolding is how you find the vulnerabilities in testimony.
fields.value_description: Three components are shown: Turn 1 scaffolding names what held the question up structurally, Turn 2 scaffolding names what held the answer up, and Emergent support names what the two turns together produced that neither contained alone.

fields.label: Question → Answer Relationship
fields.definition: How the question shaped the answer. Every question constrains what a witness can reasonably say in response — it opens some doors and closes others. This field describes exactly how the question did that: what it made necessary, what it made possible, and what it made difficult or impossible.
fields.why_it_matters: Attorneys design questions strategically. A well-constructed question boxes the witness in — it forces a useful answer or makes evasion visible. A poorly constructed question gives the witness room to wander. Reading this field tells you how much control the question actually exercised over what followed.
fields.value_description: A paragraph written in plain English describing the relationship. Read it as an explanation of the leverage the question had — or didn't have — over the answer.

fields.label: Answer → Question Relationship
fields.definition: How the answer changed the meaning of the question in retrospect. Once a witness responds, that response reframes what the question was really doing. Sometimes an answer reveals the question was more powerful than it appeared. Sometimes it reveals the question was weaker — or was being used for something other than its surface meaning.
fields.why_it_matters: Questions don't have fixed meanings — their meaning is completed by the answers they receive. This field captures that retrospective reframing. It can reveal when a witness has subtly repositioned what was being asked, or when an attorney's question succeeded in ways that weren't immediately obvious.
fields.value_description: A paragraph describing what the answer revealed about the question. Look for language about reframing, confirmation, repositioning, or exposure — these signal whether the answer strengthened or complicated the question's original intent.

fields.label: Alignment: Question → Answer
fields.definition: A score measuring how fully the witness accepted the attorney's framing. When an attorney asks a question, they are doing more than requesting information — they are proposing a frame, a way of seeing the situation. This score measures whether the witness stepped into that frame or stepped away from it.
fields.why_it_matters: A witness who consistently accepts the attorney's framing is either cooperative or being controlled — both are significant. A witness who consistently rejects the framing is either evasive or genuinely disagreeing. Tracking this score across exchanges reveals the overall dynamics of control in the deposition.
fields.scale_description: Scored from −5 to +5. Positive scores mean the witness accepted the attorney's framing. Negative scores mean the witness resisted or rejected it. The further from zero in either direction, the stronger the effect.

scale_values.-5: The witness completely rejected the attorney's framing — not just declining to answer, but actively countering the premise of the question. This is a significant adversarial moment.
scale_values.-5_to_-4: The witness strongly rejected the attorney's framing. The attorney's intended structure did not hold.
scale_values.-4: The witness strongly pushed back against the question's framing. The attorney's intended structure did not hold.
scale_values.-4_to_-3: The witness clearly resisted the framing, with strong pushback. The answer moved well away from where the question was pointing.
scale_values.-3: The witness clearly resisted the framing. The answer went in a noticeably different direction than the question was pointing.
scale_values.-3_to_-2: The witness pushed back noticeably. The answer drifted meaningfully from the attorney's frame.
scale_values.-2: The witness partially deflected from the question's frame — answered, but on slightly different terms than the attorney set up.
scale_values.-2_to_-1: The witness introduced some resistance. The answer was mostly on-frame but with a noticeable reorientation.
scale_values.-1: Minor drift from the question's framing. The witness mostly stayed within it but introduced a small reorientation.
scale_values.-1_to_0: Very slight drift. The witness was almost fully cooperative but introduced a minor complication.
scale_values.0: Neutral — the exchange neither reinforced nor resisted the attorney's framing.
scale_values.0_to_1: Very slight acceptance. The witness was essentially cooperative with minimal friction.
scale_values.1: The witness slightly accepted the attorney's framing — went along with it without any notable resistance.
scale_values.1_to_2: The witness accepted the framing without friction and answered within its boundaries.
scale_values.2: The witness accepted the framing and answered within it. A functional, cooperative exchange.
scale_values.2_to_3: The witness clearly worked within the attorney's frame, building their answer on the structure the question created.
scale_values.3: The witness clearly received the attorney's framing and built their answer directly within it.
scale_values.3_to_4: The witness strongly accepted the frame and extended it, reinforcing the attorney's structure.
scale_values.4: The witness strongly accepted the attorney's framing — the answer reinforced and extended the structure the question created.
scale_values.4_to_5: Near-complete alignment. The witness worked almost entirely within the attorney's frame with very high fidelity.
scale_values.5: Complete alignment. The witness fully stepped into the attorney's frame and answered exactly within it. The attorney had total framing control in this exchange.

fields.null_explanation: This field does not apply to this exchange.

fields.label: Alignment: Answer → Question
fields.definition: A score measuring whether the answer validated or undermined the premise of the question. Every question rests on assumptions — that certain things are true, that certain framings are appropriate. This score measures how well those assumptions held up once the witness responded.
fields.why_it_matters: An attorney builds a line of questioning on premises they believe to be solid. If witnesses consistently undermine those premises — even subtly — the attorney's strategy can erode over time. This score tracks whether the question's foundation held.
fields.scale_description: Scored from −5 to +5. Positive scores mean the answer validated the question's premise — the assumptions held. Negative scores mean the answer undermined it — the assumptions were exposed as wrong, incomplete, or contested.

scale_values.-5: The answer completely demolished the premise of the question. Whatever the attorney assumed to be true, the witness's answer made clear it was not.
scale_values.-5_to_-4: The answer strongly undermined the question's premise. The attorney's foundation nearly collapsed.
scale_values.-4: The answer strongly undermined the question's premise. The foundation the attorney built the question on did not hold.
scale_values.-4_to_-3: The answer clearly weakened the question's premise with strong force.
scale_values.-3: The answer clearly weakened the question's premise. The attorney's assumptions were visibly challenged.
scale_values.-3_to_-2: The answer pushed back noticeably against the question's assumptions.
scale_values.-2: The answer partially undermined the premise. The question's foundation held somewhat but showed cracks.
scale_values.-2_to_-1: The answer introduced a small complication to the question's premise.
scale_values.-1: Minor erosion of the question's premise. The answer was mostly on-frame but introduced a small complication.
scale_values.0: Neutral — the answer neither confirmed nor undermined the question's premise.
scale_values.0_to_1: Very slight validation. The answer was essentially compatible with the question's assumptions.
scale_values.1: The answer slightly validated the question's premise — went along with the attorney's assumptions without friction.
scale_values.1_to_2: The answer accepted the premise and confirmed the underlying assumptions without notable friction.
scale_values.2: The answer accepted the question's premise and confirmed its underlying assumptions.
scale_values.2_to_3: The answer clearly validated the question's foundation and reinforced the attorney's framing.
scale_values.3: The answer clearly validated the question's foundation. The attorney's framing was confirmed.
scale_values.3_to_4: The answer strongly reinforced the premise with clear confirmation of the attorney's assumptions.
scale_values.4: The answer strongly reinforced the premise of the question. The attorney's assumptions were explicitly confirmed.
scale_values.4_to_5: Near-complete validation. The answer confirmed almost every assumption built into the question.
scale_values.5: Complete validation. The answer fully confirmed every assumption built into the question. The attorney's framing was proven correct.

fields.null_explanation: This field does not apply to this exchange.

fields.label: Constraints Operationalized
fields.definition: The new limits this exchange placed on what can be said going forward. Once something is established on the record, certain things become harder to say, deny, or reframe. This field identifies what boundaries were created by this exchange — what is now locked in.
fields.why_it_matters: Depositions build a record that is difficult to walk back. Every constraint created in one exchange becomes a wall the witness has to navigate in future exchanges. Understanding what got locked in helps you see what lines of questioning become available — or unavailable — as a result.
fields.value_description: Each row names a constraint that became active: what class of limit it is, what type of thing it constrains, and what specifically got locked in as a result of this exchange.

fields.label: Enablements Created
fields.definition: The new possibilities this exchange opened up. Just as constraints close doors, enablements open them. This field identifies what became available — what lines of inquiry, what future questions, what arguments — that could not have been pursued before this exchange happened.
fields.why_it_matters: Good deposition strategy is about creating opportunities. An attorney who asks the right questions early opens doors they can walk through later. This field shows what doors just opened — for either side.
fields.value_description: Each row names an opportunity that opened up: what class of enablement it is, what type of action it makes possible, and what specifically became available as a result of this exchange.

fields.label: Epistemic Encoding
fields.definition: The difference between what was said out loud and what was communicated. Every exchange carries two layers: the explicit layer — the words actually spoken — and the implicit layer — the meanings, assumptions, and signals those words carried beneath the surface. This field maps both layers for each turn.
fields.why_it_matters: In legal proceedings, what is implied can be as significant as what is stated. An attorney who implies a fact without stating it creates a different kind of record than one who states it directly. A witness who accepts an implied premise without challenging it has effectively confirmed it. Seeing both layers helps you understand what was actually communicated — and what was not.
fields.value_description: Four categories are shown — explicit and implicit for each turn. Explicit items are things directly stated in the words spoken. Implicit items are meanings communicated without being said — premises assumed, signals sent, or conclusions invited without being stated outright.

fields.label: Convergence
fields.definition: Whether the question and answer moved toward each other — toward shared understanding, agreement, or a common frame. Convergence happens when an exchange ends with both parties more aligned than when it started.
fields.why_it_matters: Convergence is not always good for one side or the other — it depends on what they converged on. If the witness converges onto the attorney's framing, that is control. If they converge onto a neutral fact, that is information. If they fail to converge, the exchange produced friction rather than clarity.

enum_values.true: The exchange converged — the question and answer moved toward shared structure. By the end, both turns were pointing in the same direction. The mechanism shown describes how this happened.
enum_values.false: The exchange did not converge. The question and answer remained in separate frames — they did not move toward a shared understanding.
enum_values.partial: The exchange partially converged. Some alignment occurred, but something prevented full convergence. The 'prevented by' note describes what got in the way.

fields.null_explanation: Convergence could not be assessed for this exchange.

fields.label: Divergence
fields.definition: Whether the question and answer moved away from each other — increasing the distance between their frames rather than closing it. Divergence happens when an exchange ends with both parties further apart than when it started.
fields.why_it_matters: Divergence is a signal that something went wrong — or was made to go wrong. It can mean the witness is evading, the question was poorly constructed, or both parties are operating from fundamentally different understandings of the situation. Repeated divergence across exchanges is a significant finding.

enum_values.true: The exchange diverged — the question and answer moved apart rather than toward each other. The frames separated. The mechanism shown describes how this happened.
enum_values.false: The exchange did not diverge. The question and answer remained in compatible frames — they did not pull away from each other.
enum_values.partial: The exchange partially diverged. Some separation occurred, but something prevented full divergence. The 'prevented by' note describes what limited the separation.

fields.null_explanation: Divergence could not be assessed for this exchange.

fields.label: Emergence
fields.definition: Whether this exchange produced something that neither the question nor the answer contained alone — a new meaning, a new structure, a new understanding that only exists because these two turns happened together in this sequence.
fields.why_it_matters: Emergence is rare and significant. When it occurs, the exchange did more than transfer information — it created something. This can be a new vulnerability, a new line of inquiry, a new admission, or a new shared understanding. These moments often become pivotal points in the deposition.

enum_values.true: Something new emerged from this exchange that neither turn contained independently. The mechanism shown describes what was created and how.
enum_values.false: No emergence occurred. The exchange produced exactly what its parts contained — nothing more arose from the combination.
enum_values.partial: Something partially emerged. A new structure began to form but was not fully realized. The 'prevented by' note describes what blocked complete emergence.

fields.null_explanation: Emergence could not be assessed for this exchange.

fields.label: Change In Understanding
fields.definition: What each person in the exchange knows now that they did not know — or could not claim to know — before this exchange happened. This is a record of the learning that occurred, on both sides.
fields.why_it_matters: Depositions are information events. Tracking what each party learned from each exchange tells you whether the deposition is functioning as it should — producing real information — or whether exchanges are being used to perform rather than to discover.
fields.value_description: Two lists are shown — what the attorney now knows and what the witness now knows as a direct result of this exchange. Each item names a piece of new knowledge that entered the record.

fields.label: What Matters
fields.definition: The content from this exchange that has forward momentum — the things said or established here that will continue to shape what happens later in the deposition. Not everything in an exchange matters equally. This field identifies what does.
fields.why_it_matters: A deposition is a long document. Not every exchange carries equal weight. The things that matter are the ones that will be referenced, built upon, or challenged later. Identifying them early helps you know where to focus attention when reviewing the full record.
fields.value_description: Each item names something from this exchange that carries forward into the rest of the deposition. The arrow indicator shows its trajectory: upward means growing in importance, rightward means stable, downward means fading.

fields.label: Meaning Generated
fields.definition: What this exchange made possible that was not possible before it happened. Every exchange changes the conversational landscape slightly — it opens certain future moves and closes others. This field captures what became available.
fields.why_it_matters: Strategy in a deposition is about creating and using opportunities. This field tells you what opportunities this exchange created. For attorneys, it reveals what new questions become possible. For analysts, it reveals how the deposition's trajectory shifted.
fields.value_description: Each row names a concept that this exchange activated and what became possible as a result — what new territory opened up that the deposition can now move into.
